**Project Leopard Corridor: Budget and Work Plan**
**Document No. PLC/ADMIN/2021-001 (Rev. 1)**
**Approved: 05 April 2021**
**Period Covered: 01 April 2021 – 31 March 2024**

**1. Introduction**

This document consolidates the approved budget and the associated three-year work plan for Project Leopard Corridor (PLC). It is intended for internal planning, donor reporting, and coordination with the Forest Department and the District Administration. The figures presented here reflect the approved allocation as of the start of the project and form the baseline against which all expenditure will be monitored.

**2. Budget Summary**

The total approved budget for the project period is **INR 25,00,000 (Twenty-five Lakhs Only)**. This amount is drawn from the consolidated grant received under the Western Ghats Habitat Linkage Programme. The distribution of funds across major cost centers is detailed below.

| Sl. No. | Cost Center | Allocation (INR) | % of Total |
|----------|-------------|------------------|------------|
| 1 | Field Equipment & Gear | 6,20,000 | 24.8% |
| 2 | Staff Salaries & Honoraria | 9,80,000 | 39.2% |
| 3 | Vehicle & Motorcycle Maintenance | 2,40,000 | 9.6% |
| 4 | Community Outreach & Livelihood Support | 3,90,000 | 15.6% |
| 5 | Research & Camera Trap Supplies | 1,70,000 | 6.8% |
| 6 | Contingency Fund (Utilization Pending) | 1,00,000 | 4.0% |
| | **Total** | **25,00,000** | **100%** |

The Project Leopard Corridor budget document states the project has_budget_inr 2500000 INR. Record status: current. This figure was approved by the Project Steering Committee at its first meeting held on 02 April 2021 and has remained the operative ceiling for all financial commitments. No revision to this total has been authorised as of the date of this plan.

**3. Cost Center Narrative**

**3.1 Field Equipment & Gear (INR 6,20,000)**

This allocation covers the procurement of GPS units, handheld radios, night vision monoculars, rain gear, boots, and first-aid kits for the four patrol teams operating in the link zones between Reserved Forests. A major component is the purchase of 10 camera traps, which will be deployed in a grid pattern to estimate leopard density and movement patterns. Procurement will follow a phased schedule: 60% of items in the first year, with replacements and spare parts in subsequent years.

**3.2 Staff Salaries & Honoraria (INR 9,80,000)**

The project employs two Field Coordinators, four Trackers, and one Community Liaison Officer. In addition, honoraria are paid to 12 Village Forest Committee members who assist with conflict mitigation and awareness drives. Salary disbursement is monthly, subject to attendance and patrol report submission. The rates are in line with the State Government's minimum wage notification for skilled field staff.

**3.3 Vehicle & Motorcycle Maintenance (INR 2,40,000)**

This covers fuel, servicing, and spare parts for the two project motorcycles and the shared use of a Forest Department jeep. A maintenance log is maintained at the base office, and major repairs require prior approval from the Project Coordinator. The allocation includes an earmarked amount for the replacement of tyres and chains, expected in the second year of operation.

**3.4 Community Outreach & Livelihood Support (INR 3,90,000)**

Funds are allocated for village-level awareness camps, school programs, and the "Grazing Land Improvement" initiative, which supports fencing for community cattle corrals to reduce livestock depredation. A portion is set aside for a compensation facilitation cell, which helps villagers file claims for crop or livestock losses. Outreach materials, including posters and pamphlets in Kannada and Tamil, are also covered under this head.
**3.5 Monitoring, Mapping & Data Management (INR 1,90,000)**

This head covers the subscription and maintenance of the GPS tracking platform, purchase of large-format maps for the base office, and printing of patrol datasheets and camera-trap deployment forms. A portion is allocated for the annual calibration of 4 GPS units and the replacement of memory cards for the camera traps. Data entry support is provided on a part-time basis by the Community Liaison Officer, and the costs are included under this head rather than under Staff Salaries.

**3.6 Administrative & Contingency (INR 1,80,000)**

This covers office rent for the base office at the taluk headquarters, electricity, internet, printing, and stationery. A contingency reserve of INR 40,000 is retained for unforeseen expenses such as emergency veterinary treatment for snared animals or urgent repair of patrol vehicles. Any use of the contingency reserve must be recorded in the monthly expenditure statement and reported to the donor in the next quarterly report.

Archive item 4: Annual Report 2023: Western Ghats Wildlife Trust
Source format: Annual report

The Western Ghats Wildlife Trust (WGWT) completed its third full year of community-based conservation work across the Nilgiri and Anamalai landscapes. During FY 2023–24, the Trust focused on strengthening human–wildlife coexistence measures, expanding habitat restoration on private lands, and building the capacity of frontline village committees. This report consolidates data from our four quarterly reports and presents the year’s achievements, challenges, and financial position as of September 30, 2023.

The Trust’s expenditure for the first half of the fiscal year stood at ₹86.4 lakh against a budgeted ₹1.72 crore. We anticipate full-year spending to align with projections, subject to the timely release of pending grant instalments. We thank our donors, field staff, and village partners for their unwavering support.

---

**2. Project Highlights**

**2.1 Human–Wildlife Coexistence Programme**

The flagship programme expanded to cover 34 villages across three districts. Key activities included:

- Installation of 18 solar-powered fence units (12 in the northern range, 6 in the south).
- Refurbishment of 9 existing elephant-proof trenches, covering 4.2 km.
- Distribution of 320 chilli–tobacco rope coils and 150 reflective tin sheets to farmers.
- Formation of 4 new Village Crop Protection Committees, bringing the total to 19.

The committees have been instrumental in coordinating rapid response teams during crop-raiding events. A total of 212 rapid response call-outs were logged between April and October 2023, with an average response time of 34 minutes.

**2.2 Habitat Restoration and Corridor Linkage**

Working with 11 village commons and 5 private landowners, the Trust facilitated the planting of native species including *Terminalia elliptica*, *Pterocarpus marsupium*, and *Ficus benghalensis*. Survival rates at the six-month mark averaged 78%, with higher mortality observed in the drier eastern plots. Maintenance visits are scheduled quarterly.

**2.3 Livestock Protection Initiative**

In partnership with the Animal Husbandry Department, the Trust promoted the construction of predator-proof corrals. Twenty-three corrals were completed, and 11 more are under construction. Reported livestock losses (goats and cattle) in project villages decreased by 19% compared to the previous year.

**2.4 Community Engagement and Education**

- Conducted 14 school awareness programmes reaching 1,150 students.
- Held 9 village-level workshops on safe behaviour near elephant corridors.
- Launched a monthly newsletter, *Corridor Chronicle*, distributed in three languages (English, Tamil, Malayalam).

**7. Project Outcomes and Case Studies**

**7.1 Solar Fence Maintenance and Efficacy**

The Trust maintains 47 km of solar fencing across 23 villages. During the year, 14 km were upgraded with higher-gauge wire and improved energizers. Field teams report a reduction in fence breakage incidents. The average time to repair a fence breach decreased from 3.2 days to 1.8 days due to the deployment of two dedicated maintenance teams.

**7.2 Case Study: Mudumalai Village Crop Protection**

Mudumalai Village, which recorded 15 crop_raiding_incidents_2023, has been a focal point for our intervention. The Village Crop Protection Committee, formed in January 2023, has been active in coordinating fence maintenance and reporting. In cooperation with the Trust, the committee organised night patrols during the paddy harvest season. The solar fence along the village's eastern boundary was upgraded in November 2023. While the number of incidents remains elevated, the committee reports that the severity of damage per incident has decreased, with fewer fields completely destroyed. The committee has requested an additional 200 metres of fencing material to cover a newly cleared stretch near the Moyar River crossing. This request is under review.

**7.3 Testimonial from a Village Committee President**

"Earlier, we used to lose almost half our crop to elephants. Now, with the new fence and the Trust's support, we lose much less. The patrolling team is also helpful. We feel the Trust is with us." — Mr. K. Murugan, President, Mudumalai Village Crop Protection Committee.

**7.4 Habitat Restoration**

A total of 12 water holes were desilted and maintained in the dry season. Native grass species were planted over 8 hectares of degraded land within the corridor. A preliminary assessment in February 2024 suggests increased use of these restored areas by herbivores, which may help divert movement away from village boundaries.

**Project Leopard Corridor: Budget and Work Plan**
**Document No. PLC/ADMIN/2021-001 (Rev. 1)**
**Approved: 05 April 2021**
**Period Covered: 01 April 2021 – 31 March 2024**

**1. Introduction**

This document consolidates the approved budget and the associated three-year work plan for Project Leopard Corridor (PLC). It is intended for internal planning, donor reporting, and coordination with the Forest Department and the District Administration. The figures presented here reflect the approved allocation as of the start of the project and form the baseline against which all expenditure will be monitored.

**2. Budget Summary**

The total approved budget for the project period is **INR 25,00,000 (Twenty-five Lakhs Only)**. This amount is drawn from the consolidated grant received under the Western Ghats Habitat Linkage Programme. The distribution of funds across major cost centers is detailed below.

| Sl. No. | Cost Center | Allocation (INR) | % of Total |
|----------|-------------|------------------|------------|
| 1 | Field Equipment & Gear | 6,20,000 | 24.8% |
| 2 | Staff Salaries & Honoraria | 9,80,000 | 39.2% |
| 3 | Vehicle & Motorcycle Maintenance | 2,40,000 | 9.6% |
| 4 | Community Outreach & Livelihood Support | 3,90,000 | 15.6% |
| 5 | Research & Camera Trap Supplies | 1,70,000 | 6.8% |
| 6 | Contingency Fund (Utilization Pending) | 1,00,000 | 4.0% |
| | **Total** | **25,00,000** | **100%** |

The Project Leopard Corridor budget document states the project has_budget_inr 2500000 INR. Record status: current. This figure was approved by the Project Steering Committee at its first meeting held on 02 April 2021 and has remained the operative ceiling for all financial commitments. No revision to this total has been authorised as of the date of this plan.

**3. Cost Center Narrative**

**3.1 Field Equipment & Gear (INR 6,20,000)**

This allocation covers the procurement of GPS units, handheld radios, night vision monoculars, rain gear, boots, and first-aid kits for the four patrol teams operating in the link zones between Reserved Forests. A major component is the purchase of 10 camera traps, which will be deployed in a grid pattern to estimate leopard density and movement patterns. Procurement will follow a phased schedule: 60% of items in the first year, with replacements and spare parts in subsequent years.

**3.2 Staff Salaries & Honoraria (INR 9,80,000)**

The project employs two Field Coordinators, four Trackers, and one Community Liaison Officer. In addition, honoraria are paid to 12 Village Forest Committee members who assist with conflict mitigation and awareness drives. Salary disbursement is monthly, subject to attendance and patrol report submission. The rates are in line with the State Government's minimum wage notification for skilled field staff.

**3.3 Vehicle & Motorcycle Maintenance (INR 2,40,000)**

This covers fuel, servicing, and spare parts for the two project motorcycles and the shared use of a Forest Department jeep. A maintenance log is maintained at the base office, and major repairs require prior approval from the Project Coordinator. The allocation includes an earmarked amount for the replacement of tyres and chains, expected in the second year of operation.

**3.4 Community Outreach & Livelihood Support (INR 3,90,000)**

Funds are allocated for village-level awareness camps, school programs, and the "Grazing Land Improvement" initiative, which supports fencing for community cattle corrals to reduce livestock depredation. A portion is set aside for a compensation facilitation cell, which helps villagers file claims for crop or livestock losses. Outreach materials, including posters and pamphlets in Kannada and Tamil, are also covered under this head.

**3.5 Monitoring, Mapping & Data Management (INR 1,90,000)**

This head covers the subscription and maintenance of the GPS tracking platform, purchase of large-format maps for the base office, and printing of patrol datasheets and camera-trap deployment forms. A portion is allocated for the annual calibration of 4 GPS units and the replacement of memory cards for the camera traps. Data entry support is provided on a part-time basis by the Community Liaison Officer, and the costs are included under this head rather than under Staff Salaries.

**3.6 Administrative & Contingency (INR 1,80,000)**

This covers office rent for the base office at the taluk headquarters, electricity, internet, printing, and stationery. A contingency reserve of INR 40,000 is retained for unforeseen expenses such as emergency veterinary treatment for snared animals or urgent repair of patrol vehicles. Any use of the contingency reserve must be recorded in the monthly expenditure statement and reported to the donor in the next quarterly report.

**Field Logbook: Wildlife Conflict Response Team**

DFS-3 camera trap placed on post facing bait area. Checked DFS-3 in evening: 1.5 kg meat remaining, fruit untouched again. Leopard not photographed yet but something is eating the meat—small bites, maybe civet. Will reduce meat to 3 kg and watch.

Weekly report sent. DFS-3 use confirmed 5 nights this week. Livestock loss: nil. Good.

documents.title: Annual Report 2023: Western Ghats Wildlife Trust
documents.content:
The Western Ghats Wildlife Trust (WGWT) completed its third full year of community-based conservation work across the Nilgiri and Anamalai landscapes. During FY 2023–24, the Trust focused on strengthening human–wildlife coexistence measures, expanding habitat restoration on private lands, and building the capacity of frontline village committees. This report consolidates data from our four quarterly reports and presents the year’s achievements, challenges, and financial position as of September 30, 2023.

The Trust’s expenditure for the first half of the fiscal year stood at ₹86.4 lakh against a budgeted ₹1.72 crore. We anticipate full-year spending to align with projections, subject to the timely release of pending grant instalments. We thank our donors, field staff, and village partners for their unwavering support.

---

**2. Project Highlights**

**2.1 Human–Wildlife Coexistence Programme**

The flagship programme expanded to cover 34 villages across three districts. Key activities included:

- Installation of 18 solar-powered fence units (12 in the northern range, 6 in the south).
- Refurbishment of 9 existing elephant-proof trenches, covering 4.2 km.
- Distribution of 320 chilli–tobacco rope coils and 150 reflective tin sheets to farmers.
- Formation of 4 new Village Crop Protection Committees, bringing the total to 19.

The committees have been instrumental in coordinating rapid response teams during crop-raiding events. A total of 212 rapid response call-outs were logged between April and October 2023, with an average response time of 34 minutes.

**2.2 Habitat Restoration and Corridor Linkage**

Working with 11 village commons and 5 private landowners, the Trust facilitated the planting of native species including *Terminalia elliptica*, *Pterocarpus marsupium*, and *Ficus benghalensis*. Survival rates at the six-month mark averaged 78%, with higher mortality observed in the drier eastern plots. Maintenance visits are scheduled quarterly.

**2.3 Livestock Protection Initiative**

In partnership with the Animal Husbandry Department, the Trust promoted the construction of predator-proof corrals. Twenty-three corrals were completed, and 11 more are under construction. Reported livestock losses (goats and cattle) in project villages decreased by 19% compared to the previous year.

**2.4 Community Engagement and Education**

- Conducted 14 school awareness programmes reaching 1,150 students.
- Held 9 village-level workshops on safe behaviour near elephant corridors.
- Launched a monthly newsletter, *Corridor Chronicle*, distributed in three languages (English, Tamil, Malayalam).

Annual report 2023 reports Mudumalai Village crop_raiding_incidents_2023 15 incidents. Record status: current.

---

**3. Crop Raiding Incident Data (April – September 2023)**

The following table presents crop-raiding incidents reported by village committees and verified by Trust field officers. Data for the period April to September 2023 is consolidated from quarterly reports. Verification involves site visits and farmer interviews; some incidents may be underreported due to remoteness.

The elevated numbers in Mudumalai Village are attributed to a shift in elephant movement patterns near the Moyar River crossing, possibly linked to water availability in the dry season. The Village Crop Protection Committee has requested additional solar fence materials, and the Trust has prioritised this village for the next procurement cycle.

---

**7. Project Outcomes and Case Studies**

**7.1 Solar Fence Maintenance and Efficacy**

The Trust maintains 47 km of solar fencing across 23 villages. During the year, 14 km were upgraded with higher-gauge wire and improved energizers. Field teams report a reduction in fence breakage incidents. The average time to repair a fence breach decreased from 3.2 days to 1.8 days due to the deployment of two dedicated maintenance teams.

**7.2 Case Study: Mudumalai Village Crop Protection**

Mudumalai Village, which recorded 15 crop_raiding_incidents_2023, has been a focal point for our intervention. The Village Crop Protection Committee, formed in January 2023, has been active in coordinating fence maintenance and reporting. In cooperation with the Trust, the committee organised night patrols during the paddy harvest season. The solar fence along the village's eastern boundary was upgraded in November 2023. While the number of incidents remains elevated, the committee reports that the severity of damage per incident has decreased, with fewer fields completely destroyed. The committee has requested an additional 200 metres of fencing material to cover a newly cleared stretch near the Moyar River crossing. This request is under review.

**7.3 Testimonial from a Village Committee President**

"Earlier, we used to lose almost half our crop to elephants. Now, with the new fence and the Trust's support, we lose much less. The patrolling team is also helpful. We feel the Trust is with us." — Mr. K. Murugan, President, Mudumalai Village Crop Protection Committee.

**7.4 Habitat Restoration**

A total of 12 water holes were desilted and maintained in the dry season. Native grass species were planted over 8 hectares of degraded land within the corridor. A preliminary assessment in February 2024 suggests increased use of these restored areas by herbivores, which may help divert movement away from village boundaries.

   - Two field assistants will be stationed at the Valparai base for the first week.
